newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japanese stocks make comeback but bears still rule.
newsitem.headline: Japanese stocks make comeback but bears still rule.

text.p: Japanese stocks recovered strongly on Monday in a rollercoaster session, clawing back some of the huge losses sustained last week.

A key index had looked set to wilt in early trade, but even though it soared over 1,100 points in a dizzying rebound the market bears still clung on grimly, and analysts worried the worst was not over.
"Since last week's fall was so sharp, the index (at current levels) looked attractive and bargain-hunters emerged," said Keiko Kondo, a strategist at Merrill Lynch Japan Inc.
But Kondo cautioned that the market could again be hit by companies taking profits on shareholdings ahead of corporate book closings at the end of March.

The market started edgily, with the Nikkei average of 225 leading shares dropping close to the psychologically important 17,000 level in the morning. But broad short-covering kicked in to drive the benchmark higher.
Short-covering occurs when traders who have "shorted", or sold certain issues without actually taking delivery of them, buy back the stocks back to cover their positions.
The Nikkei, the market's main barometer, ended a hectic session up 815.14 points or 4.71 percent at 18,118.79 -- its first rally in a week.
Its March futures briefly surged nearly 1,000 points to the limit high before closing at 18,130, up 980 points.
Monday's sharp gain was more than enough to offset what the benchmark lost on Friday, when it suffered the biggest single-day drop since January 23, 1995.
It lost more than 2,000 points last week due to spreading gloom over the government's ability to keep the nation's economic recovery on track.

Analysts called the rebound "technical", however, and said it did not signal any major reversal of the bearish trend, adding that the market was still gripped by worries about the economy and the health of some financial institutions.

On Monday, the Nikkei hit early low of 17,019.56 but bounced back, supported by short-covering partly fuelled by a report that a senior official of Japan's ruling party had called for measures to deal with weak stock prices.
The call by Koichi Kato, secretary-general of the ruling Liberal Democratic Party, was reported by Jiji news agency.
But a top government official quickly denied that any bailout measures would be taken by the government.
Vice Trade Minister Tsutomu Makino told reporters that the ministry was not considering any special steps to deal with weakness in Tokyo stock prices.
"We do not expect the economy to be hurt by the recent market weakness," Makino said.
A sustained flight from stocks has fuelled fears of a meltdown on Japanese markets as investors, already deterred by low Japanese interest rates, look elsewhere for reliable returns on their money.
Brokers said the stock market was still vulnerable despite signs that the Nikkei had found a floor at 17,000 points.
Investors bought up banking and brokerage shares after last week's fall left them ripe for bargain-hunting.

Bank shares have been hit by worries that the slumping stock market may erode unrealised profits on share portfolios which the banks have been using in their struggle to deal with huge bad loans left over from the 1980s "bubble" economy.
Sakura Bank Ltd rose 90 yen to close at 740 yen in turnover of 17.05 million shares, the heaviest volume on the Tokyo Stock Exchange's first section.

The dollar hovered slightly above 116 yen in directionless Tokyo trade, barely changed from its New York close on Friday, while Japanese government bonds rose, driving the key September futures to end at 125.67, up 0.30 from Friday's close.
